svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Cloud NAT allocates ports in Google Cloud; every NAT IP address offers 64,512 TCP and 64,512 UDP source ports rather than 65,536, because the well-known ports 0 through 1,023 are never used; a gateway uses either static port allocation, which gives every VM the same fixed count and is the Public NAT default, or dynamic allocation, which starts at the minimum and doubles as a VM approaches exhaustion up to a maximum and is the Private NAT default, with endpoint-independent mapping requiring static allocation and being unavailable on Private NAT; the reservation procedure rounds the request up to a power of two, defaults to 64 ports for static and 32 for dynamic, raises the floor to 1,024 when static allocation covers alias ranges wider than a slash thirty-two, allocates double the requested minimum on Private NAT for reliability, and may span a VM's tuples across several NAT IP addresses; the ports a VM holds cap simultaneous connections per unique destination three-tuple rather than in total, so 1,024 ports means 1,024 connections to one address and port and another 1,024 to the same address on a different port; and closed connections stay unusable for the Cloud NAT TIME_WAIT timeout, 30 or 120 seconds depending on when the gateway was created, independently of the guest operating system's own TIME_WAIT
svg.title: Cloud NAT port allocation: 64,512 per address, rounded to a power of two, counted per destination
svg.text: The port count is not 65,536, the number you asked for is not the number you get,
and what it limits is not total connections.
The budget per NAT IP address
“Each NAT IP address … offers 64,512 TCP source ports and 64,512 UDP source ports.”
65,536 per protocol exist. Cloud NAT “doesn’t use the well-known (privileged) ports (0 through
1,023)”. 65,536 − 1,024 = 64,512. TCP and UDP budgets are separate, not shared.
A VM’s tuples can span several NAT IP addresses — one address need not hold them all.
Two methods, and the defaults are opposite
STATIC — every VM gets the same fixed count. DEFAULT FOR PUBLIC NAT.
“Works best if all VMs have similar egress usage.” The count “doesn’t change if some VMs use
more ports than others or if a VM exhausts all its ports.”
DYNAMIC — starts at the minimum, DOUBLES near exhaustion, up to a maximum.
DEFAULT FOR PRIVATE NAT. Ports are released when usage drops and reused by other VMs.
Cost: “while additional ports are being allocated … you might see connection timeouts or latency.”
ENDPOINT-INDEPENDENT MAPPING forces STATIC — the two cannot both be on. And EIM is not
available on Private NAT at all.
The reservation procedure — four places your number changes
1. ROUNDED UP TO A POWER OF TWO. Public NAT allocates “using multiples of powers of two, so
the number … is greater than or equal to the minimum” you set. Ask for 100, get 128.
2. DEFAULTS DIFFER BY METHOD: 64 ports for static, 32 for dynamic, if you specify nothing.
3. THE 1,024 FLOOR. Static allocation + alias ranges wider than /32 → the minimum becomes
max(your value, 1,024). A GKE cluster with alias ranges lands here without asking.
4. PRIVATE NAT DOUBLES IT — “allocates twice the number of required minimum ports per VM
for reliability.” Your sizing arithmetic needs the x2, or the subnet comes out half as big.
On GKE the tuples go to the NODE and are “shared by all Pods on the node.”
What the ports actually limit: connections PER DESTINATION
A destination is a 3-TUPLE: destination IP + destination port + protocol.
A connection is a 5-TUPLE: that, plus the NAT source IP and source port.
So 1,024 ports means “1,024 simultaneous connections to EACH unique destination 3-tuple” —
NOT 1,024 connections in total.
Google’s own example: 1,024 to 203.0.113.99:80 TCP, “another 1,024” to the same address on 443,
and another 1,024 to a different address on 80.
Which is why “how many connections do we make?” is the wrong sizing question.
TIME_WAIT: the ports you are not using and cannot use
“Cloud NAT considers closed connections to be unusable for the duration of the TCP TIME_WAIT
timeout, which can affect the number of connections in use at a time.”
Cloud NAT default: 30 OR 120 SECONDS, “depending on when you created the gateway.”
Separate from the guest OS: Linux 60s, Windows 240s. Lowering one does not require the other.
Changing your mind later is not free
INCREASING ports: no interruption, on either method. Safe.
REDUCING: static min → “no connection draining”, broken immediately. Dynamic max → breaks ALL.
Dynamic → static → breaks all active NAT connections. Set it right at creation.
